questions.q: Per this lesson, is decentralized governance a fourth reference-architecture pattern alongside hub-and-spoke and catalog-of-catalogs?
options: Yes, it is a stricter version of catalog-of-catalogs
No — it's the absence of a shared architecture pattern, not a pattern itself
Yes, it is architecturally identical to hub-and-spoke
Yes, it always includes a central index by definition
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly states decentralized is not a fourth legitimate pattern — it's defined by the absence of a shared metadata layer.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the three architectural gaps decentralized governance produces, per this lesson?
options: Excessive central audit logging
An overly detailed shared schema
No cross-domain lineage
Too many central policy engines
questions.explain: The three gaps named are no shared schema, no cross-domain lineage, and no central audit trail.

questions.q: What distinguishes 'deliberate' decentralization from 'accidental' decentralization, per this lesson?
options: Deliberate decentralization is illegal; accidental decentralization is not
Deliberate decentralization is a genuine choice for unrelated business units with nothing that needs to cross the boundary; accidental decentralization is just an unplanned default
There is no real difference between the two
Deliberate decentralization always uses a central hub; accidental decentralization never does
questions.explain: The lesson draws this exact distinction — one is an intentional architectural choice, the other is what happens by default with no design.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why is retrofitting a shared layer onto a decentralized architecture harder than designing one in from the start?
options: Years of incompatible tags and labels have to be reconciled after the fact, instead of designed consistently from day one
It is actually easier to retrofit than to design one in from the start
Decentralized architectures never need a shared layer later
Retrofitting is impossible under any circumstances
questions.explain: The lesson states the risk is reconciling accumulated incompatibility later, which is harder than designing a shared schema in up front.

questions.q: Which Foundations lesson's 'three different customer counts in one meeting' problem does this lesson connect to accidental decentralization?
options: Lesson 11 of this same course
Lesson 30 of Data Governance Foundations
A lesson that does not exist in either course
Lesson 1 of Data Governance Foundations
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly ties accidental decentralization to Foundations Lesson 1's conflicting-definitions example, now at the system level.
